question: In the 2015 Metropolitan Museum of Art exhibition titled after the Chinese zodiac animal of 2015, how many of the "twelve animals of the Chinese zodiac" have a hand visible?

history.name: user
history.content: In the 2015 Metropolitan Museum of Art exhibition titled after the Chinese zodiac animal of 2015, how many of the "twelve animals of the Chinese zodiac" have a hand visible?

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content:
Task: Determine, for the Met’s 2015 exhibition named after the year’s zodiac animal (2015 = Year of the Sheep/Goat/Ram), how many of the twelve Chinese zodiac figures in the related set show a visible hand.
Plan:
- Identify the Met exhibition page (likely "Celebration of the Year of the Ram").
- Locate the specific Met object page depicting the twelve zodiac animals (the anthropomorphic jade set is commonly referenced).
- From official descriptions and imagery, verify which figures have a visible hand and count them.
WebSurfer: Please find the exhibition page and the object page that shows the set of twelve zodiac animals. Focus on any text that mentions hands being visible or concealed.

history.name: WebSurfer
history.content:
I searched for: site:metmuseum.org 2015 "Celebration of the Year of the Ram" "Twelve animals of the Chinese zodiac".
Results include:
- The Metropolitan Museum of Art — Celebration of the Year of the Ram (January 17–April 19, 2015). Snippet indicates the show featured Chinese sculptures related to the ram.
- The Met Collection — Twelve animals of the Chinese zodiac (Qing dynasty jade set). Snippet: "The snake, for example, sits calmly with his hands in long, loose sleeves."
The object page appears to have the detailed description we need. I can open it next.

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content: Open the Met Collection page for "Twelve animals of the Chinese zodiac" and read the description carefully. Extract any lines about hands (especially mentions like the snake), and determine from the text whether any animal lacks a visible hand. If possible, confirm with the image.

history.name: WebSurfer
history.content:
Opened: The Met Collection — Twelve animals of the Chinese zodiac (China, 18th–19th century; on view in Gallery 207).
Visible text includes: "The twelve animals of the Chinese zodiac are popular decorative motifs... Qing-dynasty master carvers individualized each animal with distinctive accessories and varied postures. The snake, for example, sits calmly with his hands in long, loose sleeves. This set is from the collection of Heber R. Bishop."
Interpretation: The line about the snake indicates that the snake’s hands are present and situated within long, loose sleeves, which suggests the hands are visible as part of the figure’s presentation (i.e., not hidden behind the body). The rest of the figures in the set are anthropomorphic and typically show hands holding or folded with accessories.
From this description, none of the twelve is described as lacking a visible hand.

history.name: Orchestrator
history.content: Please click Enlarge Image on that object page and scan the high-resolution image to verify whether any figure lacks a visible hand. If any appear concealed entirely, note which.

history.name: WebSurfer
history.content:
I clicked Enlarge Image for the jade set. Observations:
- The figures are human-bodied with animal heads, arranged in three rows.
- Most clearly show hands (some holding objects, some folded at the waist).
- For the snake figure, the sleeves are long and loose at the front. While I cannot see distinct fingers, the sleeves present the hands area; combined with the description noting the hands in sleeves, this indicates the hands are part of the visible presentation, not absent or hidden behind the figure.
Conclusion from image + text: All twelve appear to have hands visible or indicated (none lacks a visible hand).

history.name: Assistant
history.content:
Synthesis:
- The Met object page describes the set as twelve anthropomorphic figures. The description specifically notes the snake "with his hands in long, loose sleeves," which I take to mean the hands are accounted for in the visible depiction (as part of the sleeves’ front presentation).
- A high-resolution view shows each figure with hands present—either holding accessories or folded at the front. No figure appears to have hands entirely concealed from view.
Answer: 12 of the twelve zodiac animals have a hand visible.

mistake_reason: Tool Output Misinterpretation (FM-4.2): WebSurfer misread the Met page’s clear text "The snake, for example, sits calmly with his hands in long, loose sleeves." The phrase indicates the hands are within the sleeves and thus not visible, which is the crucial exception leading to a count of 11. WebSurfer incorrectly interpreted this as evidence that the snake’s hands are visible, causing the team to conclude that all twelve figures show a visible hand.
